title: Changelog
text:
Implement missing .pdf features

Tables in .pdf jou mode should fit automatically.

Implement missing .docx features

Right-align equation numbers

title: Changelog
text:
Breaking changes

The apafg- and apatb- prefixes are no longer used for figures and tables. Use the standard Quarto prefixes (fig- and tbl-), as well as the standard quarto referencing syntax (e.g., @fig-myplot will reference the fig-myplot chunk.).
The include statement below the metadata is no longer used and must be deleted. An informative error will provide instruction if the include statement remains.

title: Changelog
text:
Improvements

.docx

The title page and abstract page are now processed using lua filters instead of R.
The officer package is no longer required to create a new reference document every time the document is rendered #5 #29. Now, a lua filter looks for the shorttitle field in your yaml. If that is not found, the title and subtitle fields are used instead. The running header is assigned to the description field in the quarto metadata. This value will show up in the Comments field in the rendered .docx file, which is then inserted into the field box in the header.
The .docx running header is set with a lua filter and a docx field that draws from the .docx metadata.



.pdf

Can number lines #25
Fixed tightlist error #31
The jou (journal) mode in .pdf is better supported. There are a few hacky solutions that need a bit of work. #2 #27

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
This tutorial is for graduate students who want to write a thesis or dissertation with apaquarto’s thesis mode. You do not need to be a programmer, and you do not need to have used tools like Quarto or RStudio before. If you can use a word processor and install a program, you can do this.
A few promises before we start:

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
Where are my files?

WindowsMacLinux


Open File Explorer (the yellow folder icon on your taskbar, or press Win+EWin+E). On the left you will see Documents, Desktop, and, if OneDrive is installed and signed in, an entry such as OneDrive – Temple University. That is your OneDrive folder, and it lives on your computer.
To see a folder’s full location, click once in the address bar at the top of File Explorer. It will look something like C:\Users\yourname\Documents\Thesis.


Open Finder (the smiley-face icon in the Dock). In the sidebar you will see Documents, Desktop, and, if the OneDrive app is installed and signed in, OneDrive. To see a folder’s full location, open it in Finder and choose View → Show Path Bar. The path appears at the bottom of the window.


Open your file manager (called Files on many systems). Your personal files live in your home folder, for example /home/yourname/Documents. Microsoft does not offer an official OneDrive app for Linux, so see the Linux note in Step 5.

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
What is the terminal?
A terminal is a window where you type a command instead of clicking a button. You will use one a few times. You never need to understand it deeply: you type (or paste) the exact text shown on this page, press EnterEnter, and read what comes back. RStudio has a terminal built in (a tab next to the Console), so you do not need to hunt for a separate program.

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
A quick tour of RStudio
When RStudio opens, you will see several panes (windows within the window). Their exact arrangement may differ on your screen, but you will mostly care about these:

Source (top left, once you open a file): where you write.
Console and Terminal (bottom left, as tabs): where you type commands.
Files, Packages, and Viewer (right side, as tabs): where you see your folder, installed add-ons, and a preview of your document.

If you cannot find the Terminal tab, choose Tools → Terminal → New Terminal from the menu at the top (Mac users: the menu bar at the top of the screen).

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
Check what you have

Click the Terminal tab in RStudio.
Type this and press EnterEnter:




Terminal

quarto check


You will see a list of checks. Look for these lines:

Quarto version. Does it say 1.9 or higher? If not, install the newest Quarto from the Quarto download page, then close and reopen RStudio and run quarto check again.
Typst. Quarto ships with Typst built in, so there is nothing separate to install. Typst is a modern document-typesetting tool that makes .pdf files quickly and without any extra software.
TinyTeX (under Checking LaTeX installation). This is only needed for one of the .pdf options (see the next box).







TipDo I need TinyTeX?



apaquarto can make a .pdf in two ways:








Format name
How it makes a .pdf
Needs TinyTeX?




apaquarto-typst
Typst
No


apaquarto-pdf
LaTeX
Yes (unless you already have a LaTeX setup)



If you only want .docx, .html, and a .pdf from Typst, you can skip TinyTeX entirely. If you want the LaTeX .pdf, install it as shown below.
Already use LaTeX? If you have TeX Live, MacTeX, or MiKTeX installed, Quarto will find it. You can skip TinyTeX.

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
Install or update TinyTeX (optional)
In the Console:



Console

# Install tinytex package
install.packages("tinytex")
# Install TinyTeX program
tinytex::install_tinytex()
# Verify the installation
tinytex::is_tinytex()


This downloads a few hundred megabytes, so it may take several minutes. To update TinyTeX later:



Console

tinytex::tlmgr_update()








NoteIf a pop-up or message asks permission





Quarto may ask whether you want to continue or whether to add TinyTeX to your system path. The defaults are fine. If your computer is managed by your university and an installation is blocked, contact your IT help desk. Please do not try to work around the block yourself.



When you are done, run quarto check once more in the terminal. Everything you plan to use should report as OK.

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
Formatting text



You type
You get




*italics*
italics


**bold**
bold


***bold italics***
bold italics


H~2~O
H2O (subscript)


x^2^
x2 (superscript)



APA style rarely uses bold in the body of your writing, but you might need it for a term or two. Use italics for emphasis, for statistical symbols such as p, and for the titles of books.

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
Separating paragraphs
Leave one blank line between paragraphs:
This is my first paragraph. It can run on for as many lines as I like,
and the line breaks in the file do not matter.

This is my second paragraph. The blank line above is what separates them.
apaquarto indents the first line of each paragraph automatically. Do not use the Tab key or spaces to indent.

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
Headings
Start a line with one to five # symbols, followed by a space. More # means a smaller heading:
# Chapter Title

## Level 2 Heading

### Level 3 Heading

#### Level 4 Heading

##### Level 5 Heading
In thesis mode, a level-1 heading starts a new chapter in all caps. Write headings in title case (capitalize the major words); apaquarto handles the rest of the formatting. See the writing page for how APA headings differ from level to level.

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
Making tables
The simplest table is drawn with vertical bars and dashes. Give it a label that begins with tbl- and a title after a colon:
| Scale    | Description                    |
|:---------|:-------------------------------|
| Nominal  | Categories without an order    |
| Ordinal  | Ordered categories             |
| Interval | Quantities without a true zero |
| Ratio    | Quantities with a true zero    |

: Classic Scale Types {#tbl-scales apa-note="Adapted from Stevens's classification."}

#tbl-scales is the table’s label. In your text, @tbl-scales becomes “Table 1” (and the number updates itself if you add a table earlier!).
apa-note is optional and puts a note below the table.
The colons in the second row control alignment: :--- left, :---: center, ---: right.

Typing a table by hand is fiddly. If you switch to Visual mode (Step 7), RStudio offers Insert → Table with a friendly grid. You can also build a table in a spreadsheet and copy the layout.
For more advanced users, you can create beautiful and/or complex tables with various packages in R or Python. I wrote the apa7 package, which is designed specifically for creating APA-Style tables. I wrote a 24-part series of blog posts starting here in which I recreated all of the example tables from the APA Manual.

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
Inserting images
Put the image file in your project folder (for example, in a subfolder named img). Then:
![A Simple Mediation Model](img/mediation.png){#fig-mediation width="5in"
fig-alt="A path diagram in which A causes B, and B causes C."
apa-note="Variable A indirectly causes Variable C."}

The text in [ ] is the figure’s title.
#fig-mediation is the label: write @fig-mediation in your text to refer to “Figure 1”.
fig-alt is a description of the image for readers who use a screen reader. Please always include one. It is good practice and makes your work accessible.
width and apa-note are optional.







TipWhat is the difference between a figure and an illustration?





A figure is a chart or graph. An illustration is other artwork, such as a photograph or a map. If you label an image with #ill- instead of #fig-, apaquarto numbers it separately, as in “Illustration 1.” (Check with your committee whether it prefers one scheme.)

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
Block quotes
A quotation of 40 words or more goes in its own indented block. Start each line with >:
Austen [-@austen1990] had this to say about memory:

> If any one faculty of our nature may be called more wonderful than the rest,
> I do think it is memory. There seems something more speakingly
> incomprehensible in the powers, the failures, the inequalities of memory,
> than in any other of our intelligences. (p. 163)
For a quotation that ends in an attribution, as an epigraph often does, put a final line that starts with three hyphens (---), which turn into an em dash:
> We are, to be sure, a miracle every way.
>
> --- Jane Austen, *Mansfield Park* [-@austen1990]
If a paragraph continues after the block quote (it is the same paragraph, not a new one), wrap the continuation so it is not indented:
:::{.NoIndent}
And that is why memory matters.
:::

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
Appendices
Appendices come after the references. Each one is a level-1 heading with a label that starts with apx-:
# References

::: {#refs}
:::

# Interview Questions {#apx-interview}

The questions asked of each participant are in this appendix.

# Survey Instrument {#apx-survey}

The full survey is reproduced here.

You do not need to write the word “Appendix.” apaquarto adds it, plus the letters: Appendix A, Appendix B, and so on. In thesis mode, appendices are also gathered in the table of contents.
In your text, @apx-interview becomes “Appendix A” (or whichever letter it was given).
Tables and figures inside appendices are numbered automatically: Table A1, Figure B1, and so forth.

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
11a. Install Zotero
Download Zotero from zotero.org/download and install it. It is available for Windows, Mac, and Linux. (Linux users get an archive to unpack; Zotero’s download page links to instructions.)
You will also want the Zotero Connector, a browser add-on from the same page. When you are looking at an article on a website, one click on the connector adds it to your Zotero library.

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
11b. Install Better BibTeX
Better BibTeX is a Zotero add-on. It does two things you need: it gives each source a short, stable citation key (like austen1990), and it can export your library to a file that stays up to date.

Go to the Better BibTeX installation page and download the latest .xpi file. (On some browsers you need to right-click the download link and choose Save Link As… so the browser does not try to open it.)
In Zotero, choose Tools → Plugins (on some versions and systems, Tools → Add-ons).
Click the gear icon near the top right and choose Install Plugin From File… (or Install Add-on From File…).
Select the .xpi file you downloaded.
Restart Zotero if asked.

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
11c. Add your sources
The quickest way to add a source is with its DOI (for articles and many chapters) or ISBN (for books):

In Zotero, click the magic wand icon in the toolbar, called Add Item(s) by Identifier.
Type or paste a DOI (such as 10.1037/amp0000700) or an ISBN, and press EnterEnter.
Zotero looks up all the details and adds the source to your library.







TipAlways glance at the result



Automatic lookups are good, but not perfect. Click each new source and check that the authors, year, title, and journal look right. Mistakes in Zotero turn into mistakes in your reference list. Pay particular attention to capitalization of titles and to organization names listed as authors.


For sources without a DOI or ISBN (reports, web pages, unpublished work), use the Zotero Connector while you are on the webpage, or click the New Item button (the green plus) and fill in the fields by hand.

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
11d. Find your citation key
Click any source. In the right-hand pane, you will see a Citation Key field. That is the short name you will use to cite the source. A key might look like austenMansfieldPark1990. You can leave the keys as they are. Just copy them as you need them.






NoteIs there an easier way to copy a key?





Yes. In Zotero, right-click a source and choose Better BibTeX → Copy Citation Key (the menu wording can differ slightly across versions). Then paste it into your document.

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
section: 11e. Export your library to your project folder
text:
11e. Export your library to your project folder
Now you will make a file that holds your library, in your project folder, so that Quarto can read it. You do this once, and the file keeps itself up to date.

In Zotero, right-click your library (My Library) or the collection of sources for your thesis in the left-hand pane.
Choose Export Library… (or Export Collection…).
Set Format to Better CSL YAML.
Check the box that says “Keep updated.”
Click OK, and in the file dialog, go to your thesis project folder (the one from Step 5). Name the file references.yaml and click Save.

You will now see references.yaml in the RStudio Files pane. From now on, whenever you add or change a source in Zotero, the file updates itself, as long as Zotero is open.






WarningIf you work in a OneDrive folder





Save the file inside the synced folder (see Step 5) so that it travels with the project. If you see a message about the file being in use, wait a few seconds and let OneDrive finish syncing.

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
section: 11f. Tell your document where the references are
text:
11f. Tell your document where the references are
In your .qmd file’s YAML (the part at the top), make sure there is a bibliography line that names the file:
bibliography: references.yaml
If you used apa7maker in Step 8, it may have a place to enter this. If not, add the line yourself, and make sure it is aligned with the other top-level lines, with no leading spaces. You do not need to supply a citation style: apaquarto already includes APA style.

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
Parenthetical citations
Put the citation in square brackets. This is the form you use at the end of a sentence:



You type
You get




[@smith2020]
(Smith, 2020)


[@smith2020; @jones2019]
(Jones, 2019; Smith, 2020)


[@smith2020, pp. 35--41]
(Smith, 2020, 35-41)


[e.g., @smith2020]
(e.g., Smith, 2020)


[see @smith2020, p. 12]
(see Smith, 2020, 12)



A few details:

Several sources: separate them with a semicolon. They are alphabetized for you.
Several authors: apaquarto handles the ampersand and “et al.” according to APA rules. You do nothing.
Page numbers: type a single page or a page range with a hyphen between the first and last page number. There is not need to add p. or pp., because apaquarto will add that for you. Also, the hyphen automatically will be converted to an en dash (–), as specified by APA style.
A prefix such as e.g. or see goes just before the @. If you have a prefix for a group of sources, attach it to the citation that comes first alphabetically.

Example in a sentence:
Self-efficacy predicts persistence [e.g., @jones2019, @smith2020, 35-41].

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
Narrative citations
A narrative citation puts the author’s name in your sentence. Write the key with no brackets:







You type
You get




@smith2020 found a result.
Smith (2020) found a result.


@smith2020 [101--103] found a result.
Smith (2020, pp. 101–103) found a result.


@smith2020 ['s] theory
Smith’s (2020) theory


@smith2020 ['s, 35] theory
Smith’s (2020, p. 35) theory



Notes:

For page numbers, put them in square brackets after the key. You do not need to type “p.” or “pp.” here; apaquarto adds it, and a hyphen between two numbers becomes an en dash.
The ['s] trick is an apaquarto feature for possessives. It puts the possessive on the author’s name and moves the year outside, as APA prescribes.







TipTip: Make a citation easier to spot



If a citation does not turn into a name and year, but shows up as @smith2020 in your output, the key is not in your references file. Check the spelling, and check that Zotero has the source and has exported it (Step 11e). Capitalization matters!


For more patterns (suppressing ampersands, masked citations, meta-analysis references), see the citations section of the writing page.

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
Change the YAML directly
Open your .qmd file and edit the settings at the top. For example, to change the committee or the date:
thesis:
  date: December 2027
or to change the left margin:
margin:
  left: 1.25in
The options page lists everything you can change, including the thesis options. Each entry includes an example you can copy.

title: Thesis and Dissertation Tutorial
text:
Or use apa7maker again
Go back to apa7maker, import your document, change what you like, click Make Document and Update, and copy the YAML. Then replace only the YAML at the top of your file (the part between the two lines of three dashes), leaving your writing below untouched.






ImportantBe careful about the margins and layout



Thesis mode sets margins, spacing, fonts, and page numbering to follow the Graduate School’s handbook. Changing them can make your thesis stop conforming. If you change them, confirm with the Graduate School before submitting.

title: Template Options
text:
Options are set in the metadata section at the top of the .qmd file. Quarto metadata uses YAML, a format that allows us to store data in a format that is easy to write and easy to read. In its simplest form, it has a key and a value:
If the value is simple, it does not need any quotes. If it has any characters that have special meaning in yaml (e.g., :), you will need to put the value in quotes.
Any optional key you do not use can be deleted or commented out. If you would prefer to keep the key visible but empty, you can make the value NULL with the tilde symbol ~ like so:
If you want the null value to be easier to understand, you can specify a null value explicitly:
Here is a minimal example of what the YAML metadata might look like:

title: Template Options
text:
Authors
The apaquarto uses the standard Quarto schema for authors. It has a lot of options, some of which are not needed for the apaquarto extension (e.g., fax, phone, degrees, note, acknowledgements).
The author field contains author names, author affiliations, and author roles. Where possible, specify each author’s orcid for easy, unambiguous identification.
The corresponding author is specified by setting the author’s corresponding field to true (i.e., corresponding: true). This author needs to list an email and list a mailing address in the affiliation data. Only one author can be the corresponding author. Other authors do not need to list their addresses.
author:
  - name: W. Joel Schneider
    corresponding: true
    orcid: 0000-0002-8393-5316
    email: schneider@temple.edu
    affiliations:
      - name: Temple University
        department: College of Education and Human Development
        address: 1301 Cecil B. Moore Ave.
        city: Philadelphia
        region: PA
        postal-code: 19122-6091
    role:
      - writing
      - conceptualization
  - name: Fulano Zutano Mengano
    affiliations: Universidad de Dondequiera
    orcid: 0000-0000-0000-0001
    role:
      - formal analysis
      - visualization
      - editing
  - name: Thomas Richard Harris
    affiliations: 
      - name: Generic State University
        department: Department of Scholarly Studies
    orcid: 0000-0000-0000-0002
    role:
      - editing
      - funding acquisition
  - name: Wut C. Whosis
    affiliations: Whatchama College
    orcid: 0000-0000-0000-0003
    role:
      - software
      - methodology
      - editing

title: Template Options
text:
Affiliations
The apaquarto extension uses the standard Quarto schema for affiliations.


id

A unique identifier for the affiliation. The id can be useful for specifying an affiliation shared by multiple authors:
author:
  - name: William Joel Schneider
    affiliations:
      - name: Temple University
        department: College of Education and Human Development
        address: 1301 Cecil B. Moore Ave.
        city: Philadelphia
        region: PA
        postal-code: 19122-6091
        id: temple
  - name: Renée M. Tobin
    affiliations:
      - ref: temple

name

The name of the organization.
author:
  - name: Fred Jones
    affiliation:
      - name: Generic State University
If the author is unaffiliated, list the author’s city and region/state instead:
author:
  - name: Fred Jones
    affiliation:
      - city: San Francisco
        region: CA

department

A specific division within the organization.

group

A subdivision within the department
author:
  - name: Fred Jones
    affiliation:
      - name: Generic State University
        department: Department of Psychology
        group: Counseling Psychology

address

The street address

city

City

region

The region, state, or province.
You may specify state instead, if you prefer.

country

Country

postal-code

Postal code (zip code in the U.S.)




Multiple Affiliations
If an author has more than one affiliation:
author:
  - name: William Joel Schneider
    affiliations:
      - name: Temple University
        department: College of Education and Human Development
        address: 1301 Cecil B. Moore Ave.
        city: Philadelphia
        region: PA
        postal-code: 19122-6091
      - name: My Second Affiliation


Shared Affiliations
If two authors have the same affiliation, you can type the same affiliation twice. If you do this, make sure the affiliations are EXACTLY the same in every detail. Otherwise they will be listed as different. To make sure they are listed as the same affiliation, it is safer to use a reference id to make sure that there are no accidental differences that creep in to the editing process. In this example, the affiliation information was entered once, and the id was specified. For the second author with the same affiliation, the ref field is used to reference the previously specified id.
author:
  - name: William Joel Schneider
    affiliations:
      - name: Temple University
        department: College of Education and Human Development
        address: 1301 Cecil B. Moore Ave.
        city: Philadelphia
        region: PA
        postal-code: 19122-6091
        id: temple
  - name: Renée M. Tobin
    affiliations:
      - ref: temple


Listing Authors and Affiliations Separately
If there are a lot of authors with shared affiliations, it might be easier to list the affiliations separately and specify each affiliation’s id, which can be looked up with the ref field:
author: 
  - name: Fred Jones
    affiliation: 
      - ref: temple
      - ref: tamu
  - name: Wanda James
    affiliation:
      - ref: temple
      - ref: ucb
affiliations:
  - id: temple
    name: Temple University
  - id: tamu
    name: "Texas A&M University"
  - id: ucb
    name: University of California, Berkeley

title: Template Options
text:
Author Roles
APA Style encourages but does not require papers with multiple authors to describe author roles using the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT). There are 14 contributor roles:


conceptualization

Ideas; formulation or evolution of overarching research goals and aims.

data curation

Management activities to annotate (produce metadata), scrub data and maintain research data (including software code, where it is necessary for interpreting the data itself) for initial use and later re-use.

formal analysis

Application of statistical, mathematical, computational, or other formal techniques to analyse or synthesize study data.

funding acquisition

Acquisition of the financial support for the project leading to this publication.

investigation

Conducting a research and investigation process, specifically performing the experiments, or data/evidence collection.

methodology

Development or design of methodology; creation of models.

project administration

Management and coordination responsibility for the research activity planning and execution.

resources

Provision of study materials, reagents, materials, patients, laboratory samples, animals, instrumentation, computing resources, or other analysis tools.

software

Programming, software development; designing computer programs; implementation of the computer code and supporting algorithms; testing of existing code components.

supervision

Oversight and leadership responsibility for the research activity planning and execution, including mentorship external to the core team.

validation

Verification, whether as a part of the activity or separate, of the overall replication/reproducibility of results/experiments and other research outputs.

visualization

Preparation, creation and/or presentation of the published work, specifically visualization/data presentation.

writing

Preparation, creation and/or presentation of the published work, specifically writing the initial draft (including substantive translation).

editing

Preparation, creation and/or presentation of the published work by those from the original research group, specifically critical review, commentary or revision – including pre- or post-publication stages.



It is possible to list the roles for each author:
author: 
  - name: Fred Jones
    role: 
      - conceptualization
      - funding acquisition
      - writing
  - name: Wanda James
    role:
      - conceptualization
      - formal analysis
      - visualization
      - editing
When 2 or more authors have the same role, one may specify the degree of contribution (lead, equal, supporting):
author: 
  - name: Fred Jones
    role: 
      - conceptualization: lead
      - visualization: supporting
      - investigation: equal
      - funding acquisition
      - writing
  - name: Wanda James
    role:
      - conceptualization: supporting
      - visualization: lead
      - investigation: equal
      - formal analysis
      - editing

title: Template Options
text:
Author Notes
The first paragraph of the Author Note will be populated with all the ORCID IDs that have been specified.
The second paragraph consists of status changes:


affiliation-change

Describe author affiliation changes.
Example:
author-note:
  status-changes:
    affiliation-change: Fred Jones is now at Generic State University

deceased

Disclose names of authors who are now deceased.
Example:
author-note:
  status-changes:
    deceased: Fred Jones is deceased.



The third paragraph consists of study details and author disclosures:


study-registration

Describe where the study was registered.
Example:
author-note:
  disclosures:
    study-registration: "This study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier NTC998877)."

data-sharing

Data/materials that have been shared
Example:
author-note:
  disclosures:
    data-sharing: "Data from this study can be accessed at https://academicdata.org/jones2024."

related-report

Acknowledge and cite data/materials that were used previously
Example:
author-note:
  disclosures:
    related-report: "This article is based on the dissertation completed by Graham (2018)"

conflict-of-interest

Disclose author conflicts of interest
Example:
author-note:
  disclosures:
    conflict-of-interest: "Fred Jones has been a paid consultant for Corporation X, which funded this study."

financial-support

Acknowledge funding sources
Example:
author-note:
  disclosures:
    financial-support: "This study was supported by Grant 123 from Academic Funders United."

gratitude

Authors can express gratitude.
Example:
author-note:
  disclosures:
    gratitude: "The authors are grateful to Sidney Fiero for thoughtful comments on an early draft of this paper."

authorship-agreements

Authors can disclose any agreements they entered into regarding the paper.
Example:
author-note:
  disclosures:
    authorship-agreements: "Because the authors are equal contributors, order of authorship was determined by a fair coin toss."



The fourth paragraph of the Author Note consists of the correspondence information. It will created automatically from the contact information from the author marked as the corresponding author. If you wish to override this paragraph with one entirely of your own, you can set it via the correspondence-note subfield in the author-note field.
author-note:
  correspondence-note: This will override the correspondence note that would otherwise be generated.

title: Template Options
text:
The shape of the title
The Graduate School asks for the title in capitals, and for an inverted pyramid when it runs to more than one line: the first line longest, each line after it shorter. apaquarto works the lines out for you. It measures the words and tries every arrangement from two lines up to eight, aiming each line at a straight taper — for a title of four lines, the full measure, three quarters of it, half, a quarter — and takes the arrangement that sits nearest. That settles how many lines the title wants without anyone having to say.
The lines are worked out once, in Lua, and handed to all four formats, so the title page has the same shape in the .pdf, the .docx, the typst and the .html.
To break the title yourself instead, write it as a block and end each line with a backslash:
title: |
  This is the First Line of My Title \
  And This is the Second Line
Those are then the lines, and nothing is worked out.

title: Template Options
text:
Margins
The handbook asks for 1.5” at the left, where the work is bound, and 1” elsewhere, and says the margins are “the same for the entire manuscript, including front matter”. documentmode: thesis sets them in the .pdf, the typst and the .docx.
A margin the document names with margin replaces the handbook’s on every page but the title page, the front matter as well as the body, so the whole work moves together, in all three formats. A side left out keeps the handbook’s.
margin:
  left: 1.25in
The title page is the exception: it is set on 1” all round, so that the block of it stands at the centre of the paper rather than at the centre of a text block pushed right by the binding margin. That is what the dissertations Temple publishes do, and what the Graduate School’s own template draws. The title is broken against the measure that page has, not the body’s. title-margin under thesis gives it margins of its own.
Confirm with the Graduate School before submitting on margins other than the handbook’s.

title: Template Options
section: The abstract, the dedication and the acknowledgments
text:
The abstract, the dedication and the acknowledgments
The abstract is the document’s own abstract, and the acknowledgments are acknowledgments (or acknowledgements). Each is set under a heading of its own, in capitals and centred, with the prose flush at the margin, no first line indented, and double spaced, as the handbook asks. Either runs as long as it runs and takes a second page if it needs one.
The dedication is dedication. It carries no heading and is centred, double spaced, well down its own page.
All three may be written at the top level, beside abstract, or inside the thesis block.
abstract: "What the work found."
dedication: |
  For everyone who wondered whether this would ever be finished.
acknowledgments: |
  Thanks to my committee, and to everyone who read a draft.
The Graduate School’s own template sets its abstract and its acknowledgments differently from one another — one begins at the margin and the other is indented, and the air under the heading is not the same on both. apaquarto sets them alike.

title: Template Options
text:
The table of contents
The contents lists the front matter in capitals — the abstract, the dedication, the acknowledgments — then the chapters under a column label reading CHAPTER, each with its arabic number and its title in capitals, and then the back matter: the references, and the appendices, lettered in the order they are mentioned. Page stands at the right margin under the heading, and leader dots run out to the page numbers.
Neither the copyright page nor the contents itself is listed, which is what the handbook asks. CHAPTER and APPENDICES are column labels rather than entries: they carry no leader and no page, and the chapters and appendices under them carry both.
The entries are black. They are links, and a link would otherwise take linkcolor and leave the contents reading as a page of cross references rather than as a list; toccolor says what they take instead, in the lists of tables and figures as well.
How deep it goes is quarto’s own toc-depth, counting levels of heading: 1 lists the chapters and nothing under them, 4 adds the three levels of subheading the handbook allows, and anything deeper is cut back to four. Quarto’s default is 3.
toc-depth: 1
The handbook asks that a level listed for one chapter be listed for every chapter that has it, which is worth a look before you go deeper than the chapters.

title: Template Options
text:
Chapters
A chapter is a level-one heading in the body. In thesis mode a heading reading Introduction at the head of the body is kept rather than taken out — a dissertation’s chapters are named, and that heading is the first chapter’s name.
Every level-one heading is set in capitals, and over each chapter stands the word CHAPTER and its number, on a line of its own and set like the heading under it.
Every major division begins a page of its own, which is what the handbook asks: each chapter, the references, and each appendix.
A level-one heading with a part of its own to play — the references, an appendix, the label over an appendix — is not a chapter. It is set in capitals like the rest but carries no CHAPTER line and is not counted in the numbering.
The CHAPTER lines are not listed in the table of contents, which names a chapter by its own heading. The word can be changed with thesis-chapter-label in the language field.
In the .pdf and in typst the page numbers are worked out as the document is set. In .docx they are fields, as the lists of figures and tables are, and they are blank until something makes Word paginate: select all and press F9, or print, or export to PDF. .html has no pages, so an entry there is the words and a link to them.

title: Template Options
section: The lists of tables, figures and illustrations
text:
The lists of tables, figures and illustrations
A dissertation carries a table of contents and a list for each kind of float unless it says otherwise, which is the other way round from apaquarto’s other modes: list-of-contents, list-of-tables, list-of-figures and list-of-illustrations are all true here, and the field says what to leave out rather than what to put in.
list-of-illustrations: false
A list with nothing in it is left out whatever the field says, and the contents does not name it: a heading reading LIST OF TABLES over an empty page helps nobody, and the Graduate School’s own template says as much — “if no tables, delete this page”.
A list is built for every kind of float the document holds — tables first, then figures, then anything the document declared for itself under crossref.custom. Each stands under a heading of its own, LIST OF TABLES and the rest, with two column labels over the entries: what the list is of at the left margin and Page at the right. An entry is the float’s number, its caption, leader dots and the page.
An illustration is a figure with a word and a count of its own, so it is numbered from one rather than continuing after the figures, and its caption is set the way a figure’s is: the number on a line of its own with the caption under it. apa-note works on it as it does on a figure, written either on the image or on the div that holds it, and in .docx it is given the same styles a figure has, which hold the note on the page with the illustration it belongs to. The same goes for any other kind of float a document declares.
format:
  apaquarto-pdf:
    crossref:
      custom:
        - kind: float
          reference-prefix: Illustration
          key: ill
          latex-env: illustration
Declare a custom float in each format block rather than once for all of them. Quarto drops latex-env on the way through an extension’s shared options, and its own LaTeX code then stops on the missing field.
The lists are listed in the table of contents, as the handbook asks, and are numbered in the same lower-case roman as the rest of the front matter.

title: Template Options
text:
Line spacing
The handbook sets the line spacing part by part, and documentmode: thesis follows it in all four formats.
The body is double spaced, and so are the abstract, the dedication, the acknowledgments and the preface.
A block quotation is single spaced and indented half an inch from the left margin and half an inch from the right, which is what marks it out as quoted.
The entries of the reference list are single spaced within an entry, with a double space between one entry and the next, hanging half an inch. The table of contents and the lists of tables, figures and illustrations are set the same way: a title of two or more lines is single spaced and turns over under its own first word, and a double space stands between one entry and the next.
Notes are single spaced within a note, with a double space between one note and the next and the first line indented half an inch, which is where the note’s number sits. In .html the number belongs to the list the browser draws and is left where it is; the line spacing is the same.
Widows and orphans are avoided, so no page breaks after the first line of a paragraph or before its last. The .pdf is the one that has to be told; .docx and typst avoid them already, and .html has no pages to break.
Each format takes its own single spacing — what Word, LaTeX and typst each call a single-spaced line differs by a point or so — and its own double, which is what every other documentmode does too.

title: Template Options
text:
Page numbering
The handbook asks for lower-case roman numerals through the front matter and arabic numerals from the first page of the body, and says that “the Title Page is page i, but does not show a page number”. That is what documentmode: thesis sets: the title page is counted and carries nothing, the copyright page is ii, and the body begins again at 1.
There is no running head. The number sits at the centre of the foot, which is where the dissertations Temple publishes put it.
Confirm the current requirements with the Graduate School before submitting: apaquarto follows the 2024–2025 handbook, and a handbook is revised.

title: Template Options
section: The words of the front matter
text:
The words of the front matter
Every word the front matter sets can be changed under language, for a dissertation written in another language or a degree that words things differently. A word left out keeps its English default.
language:
  thesis-committee: "Dissertation Committee:"
  thesis-list-of-illustrations: "LIST OF PLATES"


thesis-article

Default: A
The article before the kind of work on the title page: A Dissertation.

thesis-submitted-to

Default: Submitted to
The line between the kind of work and who it is submitted to.

thesis-fulfillment

Default: In Partial Fulfillment
The first line above the degree on the title page.

thesis-requirements

Default: of the Requirements for the Degree
The second line above the degree on the title page.

thesis-by

Default: by
The line above the author’s name on the title page.

thesis-committee

Default: Examining Committee Members:
The heading over the examining committee at the foot of the title page.

thesis-copyright

Default: Copyright
The word after © on the copyright page: © Copyright 2027 by A. Author.

thesis-copyright-by

Default: by
The word before the author’s name on the copyright page.

thesis-rights-reserved

Default: All Rights Reserved
The line under the copyright notice.

thesis-abstract

Default: ABSTRACT
The heading of the abstract page, and its entry in the table of contents.

thesis-dedication

Default: DEDICATION
The dedication’s entry in the table of contents. The page itself carries no heading.

thesis-acknowledgments

Default: ACKNOWLEDGMENTS
The heading of the acknowledgments page, and its entry in the table of contents.

thesis-contents

Default: TABLE OF CONTENTS
The heading of the table of contents.

thesis-page-column

Default: Page
The label over the page numbers in the table of contents and in each list.

thesis-chapter-column

Default: CHAPTER
The label over the chapters in the table of contents.

thesis-chapter-label

Default: CHAPTER
The word over each chapter’s heading in the body, before its number: CHAPTER 1.

thesis-appendices

Default: section-title-appendices in capitals: APPENDICES
The label over the appendices in the table of contents.

thesis-list-of-tables thesis-list-of-figures thesis-list-of-illustrations

Default: LIST OF TABLES, LIST OF FIGURES, …
The heading of each list of floats, and its entry in the table of contents. The key is thesis- and the field that asks for the list: thesis-list-of-tables names the list list-of-tables sets. A kind declared under crossref.custom gets one of its own, as thesis-list-of-illustrations does for Illustration; give it here when its plural is not the word and an s.

title: Installation
text: Installing apaquarto is not hard, but it takes a bit more effort than installing a standalone program. There are four main steps:

title: Installation
text:
Install Quarto
The current stable version of Quarto can be installed here.
apaquarto needs Quarto 1.9 or greater. The .pdf and Typst outputs rely on parts of Quarto that earlier versions do not have, and installing apaquarto on an older Quarto stops with a message saying so.
If you use a recent version of RStudio, Quarto is already installed — but RStudio carries whichever version it was built with, which may be older than 1.9. The check below says which version is being used; if it is older than 1.9, install Quarto on its own from the link above and restart RStudio.






NoteHow to check which version of Quarto is installed





In a terminal, run



Terminal

quarto --version

title: Installation
text:
Install a Programming Language
Your primary options are

R
Python
Julia







TipWhat if I do not want to use any programming languages?





If you just want to use apaquarto to make APA-style documents, but do not plan to do any analyses, install R and RStudio. You do not need R for anything, but the Quarto experience will be easier in RStudio with R installed.

title: Installation
text:
Install your programming environment
At the same link for installing Quarto, there are links for selecting an environment for using Quarto. Your options include:

RStudio will probably give the smoothest experience to anyone new to data analysis. It is made by Posit, the same company that makes Quarto.
Positron is made by Posit, the same company that makes Quarto and RStudio. It is inspired by RStudio but is multi-lingual by design. Positron will likely become the default recommendation on this list when it is further along in its development.
VS Code works for any language. Some R users really like VS Code, but those who do will likely migrate to Positron because Positron is a data-science-specific fork of VS Code.
Jupyter, as its name indicates, works with Julia, Python, and R.
Neovim, a hyperextensible Vim-based text editor
Any text editor will do. Everyone has options—Quarto won’t box you in.

title: Introduction to apaquarto
text:
Style guides facilitate scientific communication. Because scholars often write about inherently difficult topics, preventing any avoidable barriers to communication is all the more necessary. Style guides make information easier to absorb because it is presented in a predictable sequence and a familiar format. Still, in removing unnecessary barriers to communication on the reader’s end, style guides themselves often place unnecessary roadblocks before the writer.
APA style is fussier than most discipline-specific guides. Because it was introduced in the pre-computer age (Bentley et al. 1929), its quirks and charms resist easy automation. Even after decades of experience, I still need to look things up. Constantly. The basics of APA style are easy enough to learn, but there are a lot of particulars to keep in mind. Not only are there rules and exceptions to rules to remember, there are exceptions to the exceptions that must not be forgotten.
I wrote apaquarto so that I would never have to worry about APA style ever again. With very little extra effort, your documents are formatted according to APA style. In Figure 1 we see an example of apaquarto’s output to “manuscript mode”. Switching the document to “journal model, produces output formatted like an APA journal (see Figure 2).



Unable to display PDF file. Download instead.


Figure 1: Example document in manuscript mode






Unable to display PDF file. Download instead.


Figure 2: Example document in journal mode




Quarto makes writing scientific documents easier
The apaquarto extension is built on Quarto, an open-source publishing system specifically adapted for scientific and technical documents such as journal articles, books, blogs, slides, and dashboards, and websites. Not only does Quarto offer considerable flexibility by itself, it was designed to be extensible. Thus, Quarto can take care of most of the formatting, and an extension can be written to handle whatever specific formatting rules a style guide requires. The apaquarto extension takes care of all the fussy details of APA-style so that you can focus on the content of your writing.
You do not need to know any programming languages to use Quarto. You can use it in a completely non-technical way to write well-formatted text, tables, figures, and references. However, if your document communicates the results from data analyses, then Quarto offers you something quite remarkable. You can perform your analyses and communicate your findings in the same file! That is, you write text and code together in a source document and then you “render” the document into its final format (e.g., .html, .pdf, .docx). So instead of performing your analyses elsewhere (e.g., SPSS) and then copying the results into a word processor (e.g., MS Word), you build your document in one step.
The advantages of this kind of workflow are profound. If you discover a mistake in your analysis, there is no need to find and replace the primary results and their downstream consequences scattered throughout the document. Instead, you just re-render the document, and everything in it is updated. When the document is published, the Quarto file serves as a fully reproducible record of your analysis. Making the Quarto file available in a public repository increases trust in your work because anyone can inspect it and trace any result you report back to the source code that created it.





References

Bentley, Madison, CA Peerenboom, FW Hodge, Edward B Passano, HC Warren, and MF Washburn. 1929. “Instructions in Regard to Preparation of Manuscript.” Psychological Bulletin 26 (2): 57.

title: Web App
text:
Keeping track of apquarto’s many options can be difficult, and with each new feature, the list of options grows. I have make a small app that makes it easier to create the initial apaquarto document.
The app can be accessed here. Be patient as it loads.






Figure 1: Screenshot of apaquarto web app



The app is mostly self-explanatory. You fill in necessary information or select options that suit your purpose. When ready, click Make Document in the side menu and then click Update. Copy the resulting text into an existing Quarto file.

title: APA Style via Markdown
text:
A good place to start learning about writing Quarto documents is here. I will cover material needed to use apaquarto to write an APA Style document in Markdown text.
Markdown makes writing in a consistent style straightforward and easy. Its plain-text format was designed to be easy to read and easy to write, yet also flexible and specific enough that it could be converted automatically into fully formatted documents.
If you are used to writing with a word processor (e.g., MS Word, Google Docs), it might feel disconcerting to not see what the document will look like as you type. This feeling will pass, and the benefits of typing in a plain-text format will become evident. While writing in APA style, the plain-text Markdown approach prevents the introduction of many inconsistencies and makes it much easier to spot and fix any inconsistencies that are already present.

title: APA Style via Markdown
text:
Level 1 Headings
APA Style reserves a small number of level-1 headings with standard names:

Method
Results
Discussion
References
Appendices

There should be no level-1 heading for the introduction. The title acts as the heading for the introduction, and apaquarto places it there automatically.

title: APA Style via Markdown
text:
Levels 2–5
Readers are better able to follow your ideas if you differentiate long sections in your document with headings. I try limit my writing to just levels 1 and 2, but sometimes level 3 headings are needed. I am sparing to the point of stinginess with levels 4 and 5.

title: APA Style via Markdown
text:
What Can Follow a Heading

Anything can follow immediately after headings at levels 1–3, including other headings.
Headings at levels 4 and 5 must have text paragraphs below them. Why? When rendered, level-4 and level-5 headings appear on the same line as the paragraphs they summarize.


# Level 1 Heading

This paragraph follows the level-1 heading.

## Level 2 Heading 

### This Level-3 Heading Directly Follows the Level-2 Heading.

This paragraph follows the level-3 heading.

#### Level 4 Heading

This paragraph will appear on the same line as the level-4 heading.

Subsequent paragraphs go on their own lines.

##### Level 5 Heading

This paragraph will appear on the same line as the level-5 heading.

Subsequent paragraphs go on their own lines.

title: APA Style via Markdown
text:
Level 2 Heading

This Level-3 Heading Directly Follows the Level-2 Heading.
This paragraph follows the level-3 heading.

Level 4 Heading.
This paragraph will appear on the same line as the level-4 heading.
Subsequent paragraphs go on their own lines.

Level 5 Heading.
This paragraph will appear on the same line as the level-5 heading.
Subsequent paragraphs go on their own lines.

title: APA Style via Markdown
text:
Block Quotes and Suppressing Indentation
Sometimes you want to give a longer quote that needs to go in its own paragraph. Block quotes are on their own line starting with the > character. For example, Jane Austen’s (1814/1990) Mansfield Park has some memorable insights about the mind:

> If any one faculty of our nature may be called more wonderful than the rest, I do think it is memory. There seems something more speakingly incomprehensible in the powers, the failures, the inequalities of memory, than in any other of our intelligences. The memory is sometimes so retentive, so serviceable, so obedient; at others, so bewildered and so weak; and at others again, so tyrannic, so beyond control! We are, to be sure, a miracle every way; but our powers of recollecting and of forgetting do seem peculiarly past finding out. (p. 163)

If your quote has multiple paragraphs, like this passage from Brown (2012), separate them with a lone > character between the lines:


> In the entire field of astronomy, there is no word other than planet that has a precise, lawyerly definition, in which certain criteria are specifically enumerated. Why does planet have such a definition but star, galaxy, and giant molecular cloud do not? Because in astronomy, as in most sciences, scientists work by concepts rather than by definitions. The concept of a star is clear; a star is a collection of gas with fusion reactions in the interior giving off energy. A galaxy is a large, bound collection of stars. A giant molecular cloud is a giant cloud of molecules. The concept of a planet—in the eight-planet solar system—is equally simple to state. A planet is a one of a small number of bodies that dominate a planetary system. That is a concept, not a definition. How would you write that down in a precise definition?
>
> I wouldn’t. Once you write down a definition with lawyerly precision, you get the lawyers involved in deciding whether or not your objects are planets. Astronomers work in concepts. We rarely call in the attorneys for adjudication. (p. 242)
If the text after a quote is a new paragraph, you can create it in the usual fashion (i.e., plain text with an empty line between the block text and the new paragraph). However, if the text after a quote is part of the same paragraph, you can suppress the indentation by creating a div with the .NoIndent class. As an example:
Initial paragraph

> Block quote paragraph

:::{.NoIndent}
Because this sentence continues the initial paragraph, 
the indentation is suppresed.
:::

Attributions
To end a quotation with a dash attribution, as an epigraph often is, make its last paragraph begin with an em dash. Typing three hyphens (---) gives one:
> We are, to be sure, a miracle every way.
>
> --- Jane Austen, *Mansfield Park* [-@austenMansfieldPark1990]
The attribution is set against the right edge of the quotation with no first-line indent, in every format. It keeps its formatting, and a citation in it works as any other does. APA style cites a block quotation in parentheses after its final punctuation, as in the examples above, so an attribution is for when you want the other look.
A quotation whose last paragraph only happens to begin with a dash (the last line of a dialogue, say) is left as it is when you put it inside a no-attribution div:
::: no-attribution
> --- Where are you going?
>
> --- Out.
:::

title: APA Style via Markdown
text:
Figures in Code Chunks
Code chunk (also known as code blocks) are special sections of a Quarto document that run code. Quarto supports many programming languages, but I will focus on R.
An empty code chunk looks like this:

```{r}```



Those are not single quotes (') that fence in the code chunk. Those are backticks (`), which are usually above the Tab key on most keyboards in the US.




Figure 2


Keyboard with backtick hightlighted







Directly typing the three backticks and the curly braces needed for a code chunk can be tedious. In RStudio, use the keyboard shortcut  to create chunks. If keyboard shortcuts are hard to remember, there is a green button with a white “C” in RStudio’s toolbar that creates code chunks. 
At a minimum, an APA-Style figure needs a unique label with the fig- prefix, a caption in title case specified with fig-cap, and code for the plot.

```{r}
#| label: fig-myplot
#| fig-cap: This Is the Figure Caption.
library(tidyverse)
tibble(x = seq(0, 8, .01),
       y = dlnorm(x)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x,y)) + 
  geom_area(fill = "royalblue", alpha = .5)
```





Figure 3


This Is the Figure Caption.









Code chunk options like label and and fig-cap options are preceded by #|. They tell Quarto about how to run the code and present it the document.

title: APA Style via Markdown
text:
Graphics Devices
R draws each figure through a graphics device, and apaquarto names one for every format so that the same document draws the same way everywhere:



Format
Device
R package




apaquarto-html
svglite
svglite


apaquarto-typst
svglite
svglite


apaquarto-docx
ragg_png
ragg


apaquarto-pdf
pdf
(built in)



So a document with R chunks needs the svglite and ragg packages:
install.packages(c("svglite", "ragg"))
These are chosen partly to keep clear of R’s own svg() and png() devices, which draw through cairo. On macOS cairo comes from XQuartz, and on a machine without it a render stops at the first chunk that draws anything:
Error in dev.control(displaylist = if (record) "enable" else "inhibit") :
  dev.control() called without an open graphics device
followed by a long list of libraries it could not load from /opt/X11. If you see this, check that svglite and ragg are installed. A document in a plain Quarto format rather than an apaquarto one is on R’s cairo devices and can hit the same wall; naming a device in the document settles it:
knitr:
  opts_chunk:
    dev: svglite

title: APA Style via Markdown
text:
Notes below Figures and Tables
APA style distinguishes between three types of table notes, each of which need to be in separate paragraphs:

General Note. Contains definitions, abbreviations, and other information needed to understand the table, as well as copyright information.
Specific Note. These are notes about specific cells in the table, often in form of footnotes with lowercase letters as markers. Each footnote is in the same paragraph. The APA Manual recommends making the the footnote marker in superscript. The space that separates the marker from the the explanatory text should also be in superscript, hence the ^ ^ at the beginning of th footnote text.
Probability Note. This note explains the meanings of probability markers (e.g., * p < .05; ** p < .001; *** p < .001).

You can add a general note below a figure or table with the chunk option apa-note. The note can have markdown formatting (e.g, bolding and italics).

```{r}
#| label: fig-myplot2
#| fig-cap: This Is the Figure Caption.
#| apa-note: This is the note below the figure.

library(tidyverse)
tibble(x = seq(0, 1, .001),
       y = dbeta(x,8,2)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x,y)) + 
  geom_area(fill = "royalblue", alpha = .5)
```





Figure 4


This Is the Figure Caption.










Note. This is the note below the figure.




Notes in Formats Outside of apaquarto Documents
A user might want a note below a figure in a document that is not otherwise in APA-style. The apaquarto extension has the apanote filter that can add table notes to a non-apaquarto Quarto document. For example:
---
title: "An ordinary document"
format: html
filters:
  - quarto
  - apanote
---
The quarto line is part of it. A filter named on its own runs before Quarto builds its figures and tables, so there would be nothing for a note to attach to; naming quarto first puts apanote after that work, which is where it belongs.
apanote is a small companion extension that is installed alongside apaquarto and names a few of its filters. Nothing else of apaquarto comes with them: no title page, no APA headings, no stylesheet. The note is written in place below its figure or table and takes whatever styling the document already has.
Notes on figures and tables written in code chunks, on markdown images, and on markdown tables are all read. Which of them survive depends on the format:









Format
A figure
A table
A figure laid out in panels




html, revealjs
yes
yes
each panel’s own note, but not the note of the whole figure


docx
yes
yes
each panel’s own note, but not the note of the whole figure


typst
yes
no
no


pdf
no
no
no


gfm and other plain markdown
no
no
no



The gaps are not arbitrary. A note belonging to a whole figure of panels, rather than to any one panel, is written by a filter that runs at a later point in the render than the ones apanote names, and apanote has no way of naming that point: an extension that lists its filters as plain paths, which is what every Quarto before 1.9 can read, gets to choose only between running before Quarto’s own work and after it. In typst a note on a markdown table is lost because Quarto’s typst writer has turned the table into typst before the filter runs, and a figure of panels is built by apaquarto’s own typst code, which is not part of apanote. In .pdf the notes are set by the LaTeX machinery that comes with apaquarto-pdf, and in plain markdown Quarto builds no figures or tables for a note to attach to.
All of these work in full in apaquarto’s own formats. apanote is for a document that is not otherwise in APA style; a document that is, should name an apaquarto format instead.


Omit “Note” Prefix in apa-note
By default, the first paragraph of the apa-note has a prefix added (Note. ). If you wish to omit this prefix (i.e., for a specific note or a probability note), start the note with “NoNote” like so:

```{r}
#| label: fig-myplot4
#| fig-cap: This Is the Figure Caption.
#| apa-note: NoNote \\* *p* < .05; \\*\\* *p* < .01

library(tidyverse)
tibble(x = seq(0, 1, .001),
       y = dbeta(x,8,2)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x,y)) + 
  geom_area(fill = "royalblue", alpha = .5)
```





Figure 5


This Is the Figure Caption.

Multi-Paragraph Notes
If you need multiple paragraphs in the note, separate them with a yaml sequence.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-penguins
#| tbl-cap: Some Descriptives
#| apa-note: 
#|   - First paragraph.
#|   - Second paragraph.

library(flextable)

penguins %>% 
  select(-year, -island, -sex) %>% 
    rename_with(
    \(x) str_replace_all(x, c(len = "length", dep = "depth")) %>%
      snakecase::to_title_case()) %>% 
  na.omit() %>%
  summarizor(by = "Species") %>% 
  as_flextable()  %>% 
  theme_apa() %>% 
  valign(valign = "top") %>% 
  surround(i = ~ stat == "mean_sd",
           border.top = flextable::fp_border_default()) %>% 
  set_header_labels(variable = "Variable", stat = "Descriptive")
```

title: APA Style via Markdown
text:
Importing Figures with Markdown
Comprehensive details on importing and formatting figures with Markdown is here.
The Markdown syntax for creating a figure is
![caption](file){#fig-label}
For example,
![My Caption](myimage.png){#fig-myimage}
Note that in this context the figure label must start with #fig-. Additional information can be inserted into the curly braces. Some common options:

fig-alt An accessible description of the image. It is usually not immediately visible, but it is available to a screen reader.
width Image width
apa-note A note below the figure

For example, in the same same folder as my Quarto document, there is an image file sampleimage.png. We can display this image like so:
![A Simple Mediation Model](sampleimage.png){
  #fig-myimportedimage 
  width="5in" 
  fig-alt="A mediation model in which A causes B, and B causes C." 
  apa-note="Variable A indirectly causes Variable C."
  }




Figure 6


A Simple Mediation Model









Note. Variable A indirectly causes Variable C.

title: APA Style via Markdown
text:
Figure References
In APA style, we often refer to specific tables and figures by their order in the text (e.g., Figure 2, Table 4). Keeping track of which is which is a pain, especially if you decide to reorder them. In Quarto documents, we instead refer to their labels, which are converted to the right numbers later. To refer to the figure created by the code above, we would type @fig-myplot, which will be converted to Figure 3.

title: APA Style via Markdown
text:
Tables in Code Chunks
The chunk label must begin with tbl- instead of fig-. The caption is set with tbl-cap. I like making tables with flextable because it ports to to the .docx format without hassle.

library(flextable)

tibble(Letters = c("A", "B", "C"), 
       Numbers = 1:3) %>% 
  flextable() %>%

title: APA Style via Markdown
section: Tables and Figures Spanning Two Columns in Journal Mode (.pdf and Typst)
text:
Tables and Figures Spanning Two Columns in Journal Mode (.pdf and Typst)
When creating tables and figures in journal mode, care must be taken not to make figures and tables wider than the columns, otherwise sometimes makes them disappear (and sometimes takes large swaths of text with it). Typst output handles wide floats more gracefully, but the same option applies.
You can make figures and tables span the two columns by setting the apa-twocolumn chunk option to true. This affects .pdf and Typst documents when in journal mode (i.e., documentmode: jou).

```{r}
#| label: fig-myplot3
#| fig-cap: A Figure that Will Span Two Columns in Journal Mode
#| apa-twocolumn: true

library(tidyverse)
tibble(x = seq(0, 1, .001),
       y = dbeta(x,2,8)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x,y)) + 
  geom_area(fill = "royalblue", alpha = .5)
```





Figure 7


A Figure that Will Span Two Columns in Journal Mode

title: APA Style via Markdown
text:
Disable apaquarto processing (.pdf only)
If you want a long table to span multiple pages in .pdf format, the table might get cut off after the first page. Quarto makes .pdf tables using the longtable package, which allows for multi-page tables. Unfortunately, longtable does not always play nicely with the apa7 LaTeX package that aqaquarto uses to make .pdf documents. I have not yet found a fully satisfactory way get all of the features of apaquarto to be compatible with longtable’s multi-page tables. If you set disable-apaquarto-processing to true in the chunk or in markdown, you can get a multi-page table. The apa-note function, however, will not place a note below the table.
To disable apaquarto processing directly in markdown:
| Letters | Numbers |
|:-------:|:-------:|
|    A    |    1    |
|    B    |    2    |
|    C    |    3    |

: My Caption {#tbl-disabledprocessing1 disable-apaquarto-processing=true}
To disable processing within a code chunk:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-disabledprocessing2
#| tbl-cap: Table with apaquarto processing disabled (note does not appear below)
#| ft.align: left
#| disable-apaquarto-processing: true
tibble(Letters = c("A", "B", "C"), 
       Numbers = 1:3) %>% 
  flextable() %>% 
  theme_apa() 
```

title: APA Style via Markdown
text:
Parenthetical Citations
A parenthetical citation uses the reference label in square brackets and starts with @ like so:
A sentence that needs a citation [@CameronTrivedi2013].
A sentence that needs a citation (Cameron & Trivedi, 2013).

With Multiple Citations
2 or more citations are separated by a semicolon: [@CameronTrivedi2013; @cohen2003applied] becomes (Cameron & Trivedi, 2013; Cohen et al., 2003).


With Page Numbers
Page references (or any other suffixes) are placed after the reference. If you want a comma, you’ll need to insert it yourself: [@CameronTrivedi2013,  35-41] becomes (Cameron & Trivedi, 2013, pp. 35–41).


With Prefixes

Prefixes (with or without a comma) are placed before the reference: [e.g., @CameronTrivedi2013] becomes (e.g., Cameron & Trivedi, 2013).
If you need a prefix at the beginning of 2 or more citations, you will have rearrange the citations so that the prefix accompanies the citation that is first alphabetically (e.g., Cameron & Trivedi, 2013; Cohen et al., 2003). That is, [e.g., @CameronTrivedi2013; @cohen2003applied], not [e.g., @cohen2003applied; @CameronTrivedi2013].
Any prefixes or suffixes needing a literal semicolon will confuse Quarto (actually Pandoc). To make it clear that you need to print a semicolon, put a backslash before the semicolon: First Outer Inner Last [FOIL\;@CameronTrivedi2013] becomes First Outer Inner Last (FOIL; Cameron & Trivedi, 2013).







Warning



This “escaped backslash in front of the semicolon trick” is a hack. When you switch to Visual Mode in RStudio or Positron, it thinks you made a mistake, and it removes the backslash. If the citation above looks wrong, it is because I forgot to fix it after switching to visual mode and back. I reported this bug to the RStudio/Positron developers at Posit. I hope the bug will be fixed soon.




Suppressing Parenthetical Ampersands
Strict APA style uses ampersands in parenthetical citations with multiple authors. If you want the word “and” instead, add this field to your YAML header:
no-ampersand-parenthetical: true
If you are not writing in English, you can set “and” to whatever is appropriate. For example, “and” in Spanish is “y”, which can be set like so:
language:
  citation-last-author-separator: "y"

title: APA Style via Markdown
APA Style via Markdown
section: Citations for Articles Included in a Meta-Analysis
text:
Citations for Articles Included in a Meta-Analysis
In a meta-analytic study, all studies included in the meta-analysis should appear in the References section but ordinarily should not be cited in the text. Quarto allows references not cited in the text to appear in the References section when they are listed in the the nocite field in the metadata. All articles listed in the nocite field will be marked with an asterisk in the References section.
nocite: |
  @schneider2015intelligence, @schneider2012cattell
If marking nocite studies with an asterisk is unwanted, set the meta-analysis field to false,
meta-analysis: false
nocite: |
  @schneider2015intelligence, @schneider2012cattell

title: APA Style via Markdown
section: Masked Citations for Anonymous Peer Review
text:
Masked Citations for Anonymous Peer Review
Suppose you want to cite a previous reference of yours, but your anonymity is supposed to be protected in the review process. You can “mask” any citation you wish by setting the mask field in the metadata yaml to true. Then list all citations that need to be masked in the masked-citations field like so:
mask: true
masked-citations:
  - schneider2015intelligence
  - schneider2012cattell
If the mask field is set to false, the masked citations will print as usual. When mask is true, depending if they are narrative or parenthetical citations, they will be listed as “Masked Citations (n.d)” or “(Masked Citations, n.d)”. In parenthetical citations, it is possible to mix masked and unmasked citations.
Setting mask to true will also remove the authors, affiliations, and author notes from the title page.
The text for masked citations have these defaults:
language:
  citation-masked-author: "Masked Citation"
  citation-masked-date: "n.d."
  citation-masked-title: "Masked Title"
They can be changed to another language or alternate text in English in your YAML header. For example:
language:
  citation-masked-author: "Author masked for review"
  citation-masked-date: "Date masked"
  citation-masked-title: "Title masked for review"

title: Resources
text:
Alternatives to apaquarto
To my knowledge, there is no working quarto extension other than apaquarto that takes a comprehensive approach to APA style with output options in .docx, .html, and .pdf. However, there are other ways to automate the production of APA-style documents.

APA style with knitr and \(\LaTeX\)
The ability to automate APA style via \(\LaTeX\) has been around for some time—first via apa (APA Style, 5th Edition), then via apa6 (APA Style, 6th Edition), and now via apa7 (APA Style, 7th Edition). The apaquarto package uses apa7 to create .pdf documents. To intermingle R code and \(\LaTeX\) code in the same document, R-users could write in an .Rnw file using sweave or knitr. I still do so when I need the full flexibility of \(\LaTeX\).


APA style with Rmarkdown and papaja
Unfortunately, most psychology journals require submissions in MS Word (and most collaborators do as well). Learning \(\LaTeX\) is fun for some people (e.g., me), but most will not bother. With the arrival of Rmarkdown, it became possible to automate document production with a system that takes just a few minutes to learn.
The papaja package by Frederick Aust uses Rmarkdown syntax and does a fantastic job of creating APA-style (6th Edition) documents in .pdf and gets close to perfect .docx output. With a bit of tweaking, papaja can do most of APA Style (7th Edition) for .pdf documents.
